name: Diego Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential, so please give me both your public view and your private one. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a dozer on the bench at a large mine, shaping the edge before the next run of trucks. I check the tracks, climb in, and follow the marks the senior operator set out. I'm still a junior driver, and he catches places where I leave a shallow cut. I like seeing a clean grade at the end of the shift. Isabel and I have two children in school and a mortgage, so I pay attention to every hour on the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit of help with paperwork is welcome if it keeps the dozer on the bench instead of in the yard. The blade still meets uneven ground, and a driver has to notice when it starts cutting too deep. I wouldn't pay for a clever new system without seeing that it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This sounds close to my present job. I'm still learning to grade a clean edge, so my main fear is being the first person sent home when the mine has a slow week. My partner Isabel and I have some savings, but two school children and a mortgage can use it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking my dozer shifts and asking the senior operator to check the edge before I finish a pass. Isabel and I would put the next extra shift payment against the mortgage rather than take the children away for a weekend. I might try an AI explanation of a maintenance term at home, then ask the mechanic whether it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly level about the AI. I'm less level about a quiet mine; I know what one cancelled shift does to the family calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the edge still troubles you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corner where the bench turns toward the ramp. I can make it look smooth, but the senior operator shows me how water will run across it after rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay extra on the mortgage now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The balance is still big enough to bother me. One extra payment doesn't solve everything, but it lowers what we owe without buying a thing we don't need.

say: I'd welcome small **paperwork savings** if they leave operators time to check the bench.
I'd ask to see a new system **work on site** before trusting it.
think: My **junior standing** worries me more than limited AI when the mine has a slow week.
Our savings cover only a few months of **mortgage and school costs**.
do: Keep driving the **dozer** and ask a senior operator to check the bench edge.
Put the next **extra shift payment** against the mortgage.
Check an AI explanation of a **maintenance term** with the mechanic.
feel: **Level** about AI, watchful about cancelled shifts.
S0.quote: I know what one cancelled shift does to the family calendar.
fieldNote: Diego judges a tool by a **site trial** and by whether it leaves time for careful grading.
His early mortgage payment comes from a specific **extra shift**, not from assumed spare income.

steps.text: Keep grading the bench and checking the edge with a senior operator
Put the next extra shift payment against the mortgage
Check an AI maintenance explanation with the mine mechanic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software can plan a bench, but the first pass must tell us whether the plan fits the rock. Buying and scheduling may move to AI before a robot can run my dozer. The supervisor should compare the plan with a finished strip before changing our targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm open to trying a display once another operator has tested it. But if the office shrinks and sends the same work to fewer drivers, being junior could put my shifts at risk. I can't make our mortgage payment with a promise that efficiency helps everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to let me compare one software grade plan with the marks we use on the bench. I'd continue dozer shifts and note where the screen disagrees with the ground. If I lost a full shift each week for a month, I'd apply for a grader post at the nearby quarry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in a practical test, not comfortable with a shorter roster. The ground is hard enough to read without feeling I have to prove a screen right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down during that test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where the cut changes after the corner, and how much material has to be moved to keep the ramp clear. I'd ask the senior operator to initial the note so it isn't just my judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the quarry before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the grader job is full time and what hours it runs. Isabel works mornings, and a night rota could mean paying someone for school pickup.

say: I'd ask for a **bench trial** before AI plans become dozer targets.
I'd say buying and **scheduling** change before robots can grade the ground.
think: I can learn a proven display, but fewer **driver shifts** could cost us mortgage money.
As a junior operator, I need a senior worker to back my **ground notes**.
do: Compare one software **grade plan** with marks on the bench.
Continue **dozer shifts** and record where the screen misses the ground.
Apply for a **quarry grader** post after a month of losing one shift weekly.
feel: **Interested** in a test, anxious about a shorter roster.
S1.quote: I can't make our mortgage payment with a promise that efficiency helps everyone.
fieldNote: Diego's conditional openness appears in a **single bench trial** with a senior operator's check.
He links a quarry application to a precise **lost-shift threshold** and the family's school pickup needs.

steps.text: Test one software grade plan against bench marks
Continue dozer shifts and note mismatches with the ground
Apply for a quarry grader post after one weekly shift disappears for a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2028 can plan the bench and order parts, but my dozer still has a driver until capable robots arrive around 2031. The mine should state how many human shifts it expects then. Families need numbers, not a speech at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 45 when the planning changes and 48 at the robot date. I've only recently got steady at the dozer controls; if robots can do the blade work, I may be among the first drivers released. Isabel and I cannot cover a long period without my wage while the children are in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my brother Tomas, who fixes farm machinery, to show me basic service work on weekends, without calling that a qualification. I'd keep every paid dozer shift. In 2029 I'd apply for a paid machinery apprentice place at the quarry if one opens, and for a grader vacancy if the mine begins cutting drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first thought is a hollow feeling in my chest. Two years until AGI sounds distant until I remember how quickly a school year goes, and then 2031 is near.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your brother's lessons cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few weekend afternoons and fuel to get there. Tomas would help because we're family, but I would not ask him to carry our household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the apprenticeship itself be replaced later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if AGI handles diagnosis and robots take on repairs. I'd still learn paid mechanical work if it gives us another route, but I cannot call it a safe job forever.

say: I'd ask for projected **human shifts** before robot dozers become capable around 2031.
I'd explain that **planning and parts** change at AGI in 2028, before blade work does.
think: At **48**, my newly learned dozer skills may not keep me on the roster after robots arrive.
Our **school-age children** and mortgage make years without my pay impossible.
do: Learn basic **machinery service** from my brother on weekends while keeping dozer shifts.
Apply for a paid **quarry apprenticeship** in 2029 if a place opens.
Apply for a **grader vacancy** if the mine starts cutting drivers.
feel: **Alarmed** by how close the robot date feels in school years.
S2.quote: Families need numbers, not a speech at the gate.
fieldNote: Diego turns to **family instruction** for first exposure, while drawing a boundary against relying on relatives for bills.
He knows mechanical work may face **AGI diagnosis** and later robots, yet still seeks a paid apprenticeship.

steps.text: Learn basic machinery service from his brother on weekends
Keep taking paid dozer shifts while the mine staffs them
Apply for a paid quarry machinery apprenticeship in 2029 if offered
Apply for a grader vacancy if mine driver shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years is time to run a proper apprenticeship, with wages and real machines. AGI in 2031 could do the bench plans; robots around 2034 could move the dozer itself. I would ask the company which workshop roles it expects to keep paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 when thinking AI arrives and 51 when robots become capable. Our children would be older, so school pickup may change, but I don't know how much of the mortgage will be left. A workshop certificate would help only if there are actual vacancies after I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask the mine next spring for a wage-paid mechanical apprenticeship. Before enrolling, I'd spend two approved days in the workshop to see the job. In 2032 I'd apply for paid equipment service posts if my dozer hours were being reduced, including at the quarry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the fast case. I would have time to find out whether I can do the workshop work properly instead of grabbing the first course leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the fitter lets a learner handle real jobs after safety training, not only watch. I learn slowly with new screens, but I can follow a demonstration at the machine and repeat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait for the mine's course before looking elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask the quarry as well if the mine gave no dates. I'd rather take a paid opening from a private employer than hold out for a promise of help that never becomes a job.

say: I'd ask for a **wage-paid apprenticeship** on real equipment before robot dozers arrive around 2034.
I'd say **bench planning** changes at AGI in 2031, ahead of physical driving.
think: At **51**, older children do not guarantee a cleared mortgage or a workshop vacancy.
A certificate matters only if I can find **paid service work** afterward.
do: Keep driving while asking for a **mechanical apprenticeship** next spring.
Spend two approved days in the **workshop** before enrolling.
Apply for paid **equipment service** posts in 2032 if dozer hours fall.
feel: **Concerned**, with time to judge a real workshop role.
S3.quote: I would have time to find out whether I can do the workshop work properly instead of grabbing the first course leaflet.
fieldNote: The longer warning lets Diego test a **workshop placement** before committing to formal training.
He values **paid private employment** and asks about actual vacancies rather than treating a certificate as a guarantee.

steps.text: Keep driving dozer shifts while seeking a mechanical apprenticeship
Enter a wage-paid mechanical apprenticeship if offered
Apply for paid equipment service posts in 2032 if dozer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives an employer time to train people who already turn up for shifts. AGI might do plans and records by 2036; capable robots could grade the bench around 2039. The mine should tell us when new equipment is ordered so apprentices can finish before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at AGI and 56 at the robot date. Our children would be grown, but I cannot count on an empty mortgage or a pension at 56. I would need a job I could still do safely, and I'm not sure how many workshop jobs robots would leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the dozer and apply for a paid workshop apprenticeship in the next intake if the mine offers one. Isabel and I would use reliable overtime to pay down the mortgage rather than increase our spending. In 2037 I'd apply for paid service jobs at the mine and nearby quarry if I had the qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade feels workable, though I would miss driving the blade along a clean edge. I'd like the children to see me learn something hard, even if they are adults by the time the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the qualification make you feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me more useful, not secure. AGI could do diagnosis and robots could do many repairs by 2039; I would keep checking what paid work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children as they choose work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep their word to an employer and learn more than one thing. I wouldn't tell them there is one safe trade, because I can't see that far ahead.

say: I'd ask the mine to publish **equipment orders** early enough for current workers to finish training.
I'd explain that **plans and records** change by 2036 before robot grading around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still have a mortgage and no pension to live on.
Workshop skills could help, but **robot repairs** may reduce those jobs too.
do: Stay on the **dozer** while applying for a paid workshop apprenticeship if offered.
Use reliable **overtime** to pay down the mortgage with Isabel.
Apply for paid **service jobs** in 2037 if qualified.
feel: **Hopeful** about time to learn, sad about leaving skilled grading.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell them there is one safe trade, because I can't see that far ahead.
fieldNote: Diego sees the decade as time for **paid workplace training**, not a route to early retirement.
He wants his children to value work while acknowledging **uncertainty** about any trade's future.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer while seeking paid workshop training
Enter the mine paid workshop apprenticeship if offered
Use reliable overtime to reduce the mortgage balance
Apply for paid service jobs in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A robot dozer could arrive around 2031 while the children are still in school and I have barely settled into this trade. A paid apprenticeship on real equipment and an honest count of future jobs would help me choose a route while I can still earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who teaches a new operator once the old hands leave. I learned more from a senior driver correcting one cut than from a stack of instructions. If a mine offers training, it should put an experienced worker beside the learner.

headlineQuote: I learned more from a senior driver correcting one cut than from a stack of instructions.
portrait: Diego is a **43-year-old junior miner** learning to grade a bench with a dozer.
He and Isabel support two **school-age children** and a mortgage with several months of expenses saved.
He sometimes uses AI, but trusts technology after **on-site testing** and a senior worker's explanation.
He prefers **paid apprenticeships** and family help while keeping work, and fears the fast robot timetable most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Diego little time before capable robot dozers could threaten his wages around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** on real equipment and honest future job numbers would help him choose another route.
